messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always been a driven journalist, but that was before the police brutality he witnessed during a protest two years ago. The event had left him shaken, and the memories still felt more real and vivid than any ordinary memory. When trying to explain what happened, Kofi would often lose his train of thought, unable to finish the story. He would hear the sound of footsteps behind him, like the ones he heard that day, and it would transport him back to the scene. Those footsteps became one of many triggers for Kofi's maladaptive strategies. To avoid being noticed, he started wearing concealing clothing, even in his own neighborhood. He also found himself avoiding anything that reminded him of the event or the friends he had lost during the protest. Certain songs that were popular at the time would bring back memories, and he would quickly change the station. Kofi was aware that these strategies might seem irrational to others, but to him, they felt like necessary precautions. As Kofi's avoidance behaviors intensified, so did his sense of threat. He began to have difficulty concentrating on his work, constantly looking over his shoulder to check if someone was following him. Unfamiliar places became sources of anxiety, as he couldn't assess the danger lurking around every corner. Footsteps behind him would make him jump, and certain songs would send his mind racing back to the traumatic event. Kofi's memories of that day continued to haunt him. The more real they felt, the more he struggled to process them. He became convinced that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him as a journalist and a person. This negative self-appraisal fueled his avoidance behaviors, making it harder for him to engage with the world around him. As Kofi's negative appraisals deepened, so did his sense of threat. He started to see danger everywhere, even in familiar places. His memories of the event became increasingly vivid, and he would find himself reliving them in his mind. The sound of footsteps or certain songs could trigger these memories, sending him spiraling back into a world of fear and anxiety. Kofi's relationship with his partner began to suffer as a result of his maladaptive strategies. His partner would try to encourage him to go out, to engage with the world again, but Kofi was too afraid. He felt like he was losing himself in the process, that the trauma had taken away his happiness and his sense of purpose. Despite his best efforts, Kofi couldn't shake off the feeling that his life was no longer his own. The trauma had left him feeling lost and helpless, unable to concentrate or connect with others. His memories of that day continued to haunt him, a constant reminder of what he had lost. As he sat in his darkened apartment, surrounded by the silence and the shadows, Kofi knew he needed help to break free from this cycle of fear and avoidance. It was only when Kofi's editor threatened to fire him due to his lack of productivity that he realized he couldn't keep living like this. He finally sought out therapy, hoping to find a way to overcome his trauma and reclaim his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, Kofi felt a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, he could learn to manage his triggers, confront his negative appraisals, and rebuild his sense of self.
